metadata.title: Ginger-based formulations for allergic rhinitis disease: a systematic review and meta-analysis of experimental studies in animals and humans

sections.text: Abstract Background Allergic rhinitis is a chronic non-communicable disease that adversely affects respiratory health and quality of life. Ginger-based formulations, owing to their anti-inflammatory and immunomodulatory properties, may offer a promising alternative therapeutic option. Objective To systematically review and meta-analyze evidence from animal studies and human randomized controlled trials assessing the efficacy of ginger-based formulations in allergic rhinitis. Methods A systematic search of the Cochrane Library, Embase, PubMed, and Scopus (April 2025) identified studies comparing ginger-based formulations with control interventions. Outcomes included clinical symptoms and relevant biomarkers. Risk of bias was assessed using the SYRCLE tool for animal studies and RoB2 for human studies. Meta-analyses were conducted using random-effects models, with results expressed as standardized mean difference (SMD) and 95% confidence intervals (CIs). Results Twenty-one studies (6 animal and 15 human studies) were included. In rodents, ginger-based formulations significantly reduced nasal rubbing (SMD = −1.99; 95%CI, −3.15 to −0.83), sneezing (SMD = −1.99; 95%CI, −2.78 to −1.20), and biomarkers (IL-4, IL-5, and OVA-specific IgE). In humans, ginger-based formulations significantly improved itching (SMD = −0.51; 95%CI, −0.79 to −0.24), runny nose (SMD = −0.59; 95%CI, −0.87 to −0.30), sneezing (SMD = −0.56; 95%CI, −0.75 to −0.37), total nasal symptom scores (SMD = −0.63; 95%CI, −1.00 to −0.26), and quality of life (SMD = −0.56; 95%CI, −0.87 to −0.24), and eosinophil levels. Conclusion Ginger-based formulations improve symptoms and biomarkers of allergic rhinitis in both animal and human studies. As many interventions are multi-component, the observed effects are more appropriately attributed to the overall formulations rather than ginger alone. Further research is needed to explore mechanisms and clarify clinical applications.

Allergic rhinitis is a chronic non-communicable disease (NCD) characterized by inflammation of the nasal mucosa triggered by exposure to allergens (Eifan and Durham 2016 ). It is characterized by a constellation of symptoms, including sneezing, nasal itching, runny nose, and nasal congestion (Eifan and Durham 2016 ). In addition to these symptoms, patients may exhibit nasal rubbing and impaired quality of life due to sleep disturbances, cognitive dysfunction, and reduced productivity (Shaqran et al. 2024 ). Allergic rhinitis is a global health concern, affecting a substantial portion of the world’s population (Savouré et al. 2022 ; Khaki Vaighan et al. 2024 ). Its prevalence varies geographically, but it is estimated to affect between 10% and 40% of the general population worldwide, with increasing trends observed in both developed and developing countries (Savouré et al. 2022 ; Khaki Vaighan et al. 2024 ; Shaqran et al. 2024 ). The pathogenesis of allergic rhinitis is primarily an immunoglobulin E (IgE)-mediated hypersensitivity reaction (Eifan and Durham 2016 ; Bousquet et al. 2020 ). Upon initial exposure, allergens sensitize the immune system, leading to the activation of T helper (T H ) cells, particularly a skewing toward T helper 2 (T H 2) responses, which promote the production of allergen-specific IgE antibodies, including ovalbumin (OVA)-specific IgE in experimental models (Bousquet et al. 2020 ; Sharma et al. 2024 ). T helper 1 (T H 1) responses may also be involved but are typically less dominant in the early phase. The T H 2 cytokine interleukin-4 (IL-4) plays a critical role by driving IgE class switching in B cells. These IgE antibodies bind to Fc receptors on the surface of mast cells and basophils (Bousquet et al. 2020 ; Sharma et al. 2024 ). Subsequent re-exposure to the same allergen triggers cross-linking of IgE molecules, leading to the degranulation of these cells and the rapid release of preformed inflammatory mediators (e.g., histamine) (Eifan and Durham 2016 ; Bousquet et al. 2020 ). This immediate phase is followed by a late-phase reaction, characterized by the recruitment and infiltration of inflammatory cells, particularly eosinophils, neutrophils, and lymphocytes, along with increased secretion of type 2 cytokines such as IL-4 and interleukin-5 (IL-5), which sustain inflammation and promote persistent symptoms and tissue remodeling (Eifan and Durham 2016 ; Bousquet et al. 2020 ). Prevention and management strategies for allergic rhinitis involve a combination of non-pharmacological and pharmacological approaches aimed at minimizing allergen exposure and controlling symptoms. Non-pharmacological management of allergic rhinitis involves allergen avoidance (e.g., using high-efficiency particulate air (HEPA) filters, special bedding) and nasal irrigation with saline. The direct impact of lifestyle factors such as diet and exercise is still under research (Fokkens et al. 2020 ). Pharmacological treatments, used when avoidance is insufficient, include antihistamines (preferably second-generation for their better safety profile) to reduce sneezing, itching, and runny nose (Wallace et al. 2008 ), and intranasal corticosteroids (INCS), considered the most effective for reducing nasal inflammation and congestion (Scadding et al. 2017 ). Leukotriene receptor antagonists (LTRAs) target inflammatory mediators, benefiting patients with co-existing asthma (Wallace et al. 2008 ). Cromolyn sodium, a mast cell stabilizer, can prevent mediator release with prophylactic use (Wallace et al. 2008 ). Lastly, allergen-specific immunotherapy (AIT), gradually induces tolerance to allergens (Cox et al. 2011 ). Ultimately, prompt implementation of these strategies, whether non-pharmacological or pharmacological, is crucial for preventing disease progression, reducing symptom severity, and improving patient quality of life. While conventional treatments for allergic rhinitis, such as antihistamines, corticosteroids, and decongestants, are effective in managing symptoms, they may be associated with side effects or may not be suitable for all individuals (Abdullah et al. 2022 ). Consequently, there is growing interest in exploring nutrition-based and plant-derived approaches that may offer safer long-term support (Abdullah et al. 2022 ). From a nutrition and food science perspective, dietary factors and bioactive food components may play a role in modulating allergic responses. Zingiber officinale , commonly known as ginger, is one of the herbs included in these formulations and is a widely used spice and traditional medicine with a long history of use in various cultures for its purported medicinal properties (Bode and Dong 2011 ). Ginger contains bioactive compounds, particularly gingerols and shogaols, which have demonstrated potent anti-inflammatory, antioxidant, and immunomodulatory effects (Bode and Dong 2011 ; Lalruatfela et al. 2023 ; Khaki Vaighan et al. 2024 ). These properties suggest that ginger may hold therapeutic potential in mitigating the inflammatory cascade associated with allergic rhinitis (Bode and Dong 2011 ; Lalruatfela et al. 2023 ; Khaki Vaighan et al. 2024 ). Review articles (Lalruatfela et al. 2023 ; Khaki Vaighan et al. 2024 ; Lim et al. 2024 ) consistently highlight ginger’s anti-allergic effects by qualitatively synthesizing evidence from various study types. These reviews discuss findings at the cellular level, indicating that ginger and its active compounds can inhibit mast cell degranulation and reduce the release of pro-inflammatory cytokines, thereby suppressing allergic responses (Lalruatfela et al. 2023 ; Khaki Vaighan et al. 2024 ). In animals, reviews report that ginger has shown efficacy in alleviating symptoms like sneezing and nasal rubbing, decreasing mast cell infiltration in nasal mucosa, and lowering serum IgE levels in allergic rhinitis models (Lalruatfela et al. 2023 ; Khaki Vaighan et al. 2024 ). Furthermore, human studies summarized in these reviews generally suggest that ginger-based formulations may improve nasal symptoms and quality of life in allergic rhinitis patients, often with a favorable safety profile compared to some conventional medications (Lalruatfela et al. 2023 ; Khaki Vaighan et al. 2024 ; Lim et al. 2024 ). These collective findings, as presented in comprehensive review articles, provide promising preliminary evidence for ginger’s potential as an alternative treatment for allergic rhinitis. However, only a limited number of studies have investigated ginger in the treatment of allergic rhinitis, most of which focus on multi-plant formulations or recipes that include ginger as a component. Given the growing interest in natural remedies and the promising preliminary evidence regarding the anti-allergic properties of ginger-based formulations, this study aims to conduct a systematic review and meta-analysis to comprehensively evaluate their efficacy in allergic rhinitis. Specifically, the review will synthesize findings from both animal studies and human randomized controlled trials (RCTs), identify patterns, assess the overall strength of evidence, and provide a clearer understanding of the potential role of ginger-based formulations as interest in natural health products and functional foods for allergic rhinitis management.

The research protocol was established in accordance with the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses Protocol (PRISMA-P) 2015 statement. It is officially registered with the International Prospective Register of Systematic Reviews (PROSPERO) under registration number CRD42025648162. Furthermore, the Research Ethics Committee of the Faculty of Medicine, Chiang Mai University provided an exempt research determination (No. EXEMPTION 0114/2025). For the purpose of this study, ‘ginger-based formulations’ were defined as interventions in which ginger is included as a component, encompassing both single-herb preparations (e.g., extracts, powders, or isolated constituents) and multi-component formulations where ginger is combined with other ingredients. Between August 2024 and a final update in April 2025, extensive electronic searches were executed from database inception across the Cochrane Library, Embase, PubMed, and Scopus, encompassing all languages. The search strategy meticulously combined terms related to the study population (e.g., rhinitis, allergic rhinitis, allergic rhinopathy, seasonal allergic rhinitis, perennial allergic rhinitis, persistent allergic rhinitis, or intermittent allergic rhinitis) and the interventions (e.g., ginger, Zingiber officinale , zingiber, zingiberis, zingiberene, gingerols, shogaols, zingerone, gingerenone, So-Cheong-Ryong-Tang, SCRT, Xiao-Qing-Long-Tang, Sho-seiryo-to, Aller-7, Benjakul, BJK, Prabchompoothaweep, PRW, Bojungikgi-tang, BJK, Tian Jiu, or TJ) which were combined using the ‘AND’ operator. To ensure thoroughness, a manual search of reference lists from pertinent articles also supplemented the electronic searches.

The selection process involved assessing research articles that reported changes in allergic rhinitis markers following ginger-based formulations, starting with title and abstract screening. Only RCTs conducted in animals or humans, comparing ginger-based formulations to placebo or drug group were included. There were no restrictions on the specific allergic rhinitis-related parameters evaluated. Conversely, studies without a control group, as well as non-research formats like reviews, case reports, expert opinions, conference proceedings, and book chapters were excluded.

The data extraction process was independently carried out by two reviewers, and any disagreements were resolved through consensus. Details systematically collected included the lead author’s name, journal and year of publication, study site, participant demographics, comprehensive intervention information (including ginger-based formulations), intervention duration, sample size per group, and allergic rhinitis outcome measures such as itching, nasal congestion, nasal rubbing, rhinorrhea, sneezing, total nasal symptom score, quality of life, IL-4, IL-5, total IgE, OVA-specific IgE, and eosinophil counts. Corresponding authors were contacted for clarification when information in the original publications was unclear, and WebPlotDigitizer was employed for the extraction of data presented in graphical formats. The data extraction process specifically focused on obtaining change-from-baseline values (or data required for their calculation) along with their standard deviations (SD) for the relevant outcomes. For studies that compared various ginger dosages against a single control group, all ginger groups were pooled for a unified comparison. Conversely, if studies presented multiple ginger dosages, each with its own matched control group, averaging of the ginger-based formulation dosages was not required.

The systematic review center for laboratory animal experimentation (SYRCLE)’s tool, consisting of 10 entries across six domains (selection, performance, detection, attrition, reporting, and other biases), was employed to assess the risk of bias in animal studies. For RCTs, the revised tool to assess risk of bias in randomized trials (RoB2) was utilized, evaluating potential bias across five domains: randomization process, deviations from intended interventions, missing outcome data, outcome measurement, and selective reporting of results. Animal studies were subsequently categorized as having a low, unclear, or high risk of bias, while human studies were classified as having a low risk of bias, some concerns, or a high risk of bias.

Evidence quality in the study was evaluated using the grading of recommendations assessment, development and evaluation (GRADE) approach, which considers factors that can either decrease certainty (such as risk of bias, inconsistency, indirectness, imprecision, and publication bias) or increase it (including a large magnitude of effect, a dose-response gradient, and the impact of plausible residual confounding). The resulting evidence quality was classified as high, moderate, low, or very low.

Meta-analyses were utilized in R Studio (version 2025.05.1, build 513, Posit Software, PBC, Boston, MA). Random-effects meta-analysis were analyzed with ‘meta’ package (version 8.1-0), performed based on the restricted maximum-likelihood method, with statistical significance defined as p < 0.05. For quantitative variables, descriptive statistics included mean and SD, and effect sizes were summarized as standardized mean differences (SMD) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs). Heterogeneity was evaluated using Cochran’s Q and I 2 tests. Visualizations, including forest and funnel plots, were created with ‘meta’ (version 8.1-0). To detect small-study effects and publication bias, Egger’s test assessed funnel plot asymmetry. Furthermore, a sensitivity analysis explored various estimation models (Dersimonian-Laird, Paule-Mandel, Maximum-likelihood, Hunter-Schmidt, Sidik-Jonkman, Hedges, and Empirical Bayes), excluding studies with a high risk of bias, to identify the most suitable random-effects model component. During the data analysis, if mean and SD values were not directly provided, conversions from alternative metrics such as median and interquartile range (IQR) were carried out for each outcome. Missing SD values were addressed either through imputation methods or by calculation from standard error (SE) or CIs, as appropriate. In some instances, a correlation coefficient (r) was employed to estimate the SD of the change from baseline. A default value of 0.5 (Khan 2020 ) was utilized if the specific correlation coefficients for each outcome could not be computed from available data. Primary analysis was intervention compared with placebo, whereas secondary analysis was intervention compared with drug. To investigate potential sources of variation stemming from participant covariates or intervention characteristics, subgroup analyses were route of administration, categorized into ‘Oral’ and ‘Topical’.

Our search yielded 1210 articles, with 279 excluded as duplicates. The subsequent title and abstract screening of 931 articles resulted in 89 being selected for full-text review. Finally, a total of 21 articles (6 animal studies and 15 human studies) were identified as eligible for inclusion ( Figure 1 ).

sections.section: Study Characteristics And Risk Of Bias Assessment
sections.text: A total of 21 articles were included in the analysis, all of which examined outcomes related to allergic rhinitis. Six animal studies of OVA-induced allergic rhinitis were predominantly established in mice ( n = 4) and rats ( n = 2). Oral administration was the most common route ( n = 5) with one study employing acupoint herbal patching. The duration of intervention varied, ranging from 6 to 35 days. Outcome measures consistently assessed allergic rhinitis symptoms such as rubbing and sneezing, along with immunological markers including IL-4, IL-5, IgE, and OVA-specific IgE ( Table 1 ). A total of 15 human studies were included in the analysis. The study locations most in Asia, with significant representation from China ( n = 4) and Thailand ( n = 3). The routes of administration were two types, with oral administration being the most frequent ( n = 12). Acupoint herbal patching was also a notable route in several studies ( n = 3). The duration of interventions varied considerably, ranging from as short as 7 days to as long as 365 days. Outcomes consistently focused on the alleviation of allergic rhinitis symptoms, including nasal congestion, runny nose, sneezing, and itching, often summarized as a total nasal symptom score. Beyond symptomatic relief, several studies also investigated immunological markers including IgE levels and eosinophil counts. Furthermore, a significant number of studies assessed the quality of life of participants, indicating a holistic approach to evaluating treatment efficacy ( Table 2 ). Risk of bias assessments revealed that among animal studies, three were deemed high risk and three unclear risk ( Table 1 ). In human studies, eight were categorized as high risk of bias, four showed some concerns, and three were found to have a low risk of bias ( Table 2 ).

sections.section: Effect Of Ginger-Based Formulations On Allergic Rhinitis Parameters
sections.text: In animal studies, ginger-based formulations led to a significant reduction in the allergic rhinitis symptom of rubbing (SMD = −1.9899; 95% CI, −3.1537 to −0.8260, p-value = 0.0008), though the sneezing symptom showed no significant change compared to controls. Furthermore, among allergic rhinitis-related markers, IL-4 (SMD = −2.6014; 95% CI, −4.7307 to −0.4721, p-value = 0.0166), IL-5 (SMD = −2.4883; 95% CI, −4.7118 to −0.2648, p-value = 0.0283), and OVA-specific IgE (SMD = −4.4135; 95% CI, −5.2828 to −3.5441, p-value <0.0001) significantly decreased, while other markers remained unchanged ( Figure 2(A) and Supplementary Figures 1–6 ). Human studies revealed that ginger-based formulations led to significant improvements across multiple allergic rhinitis symptoms compared to placebo. These included reductions in itching (SMD = −0.5112; 95% CI, −0.7874 to −0.2350, p-value = 0.0003), runny nose (SMD = −0.5867; 95% CI, −0.8694 to −0.3040, p-value <0.0001), sneezing (SMD = −0.5598; 95% CI, −0.7471 to −0.3725, p-value = <0.0001), total nasal symptom (SMD = −0.6306; 95% CI, −1.0031 to −0.2580, p-value = 0.0009), quality of life (SMD = −0.5569; 95% CI, −0.8742 to −0.2395, p-value = 0.0006). No other symptoms demonstrated significant changes. Furthermore, a significant decrease in eosinophil counts was observed among allergic rhinitis-related markers (SMD = −0.2289; 95% CI, −0.4492 to −0.0086, p-value = 0.0417), while other markers showed no significant change. Moreover, when compared with drug, ginger-based formulation showed no significant change in all allergic rhinitis symptoms and allergic rhinitis-related markers ( Figure 2(B) and Supplementary Figures 7–20 ).

The sensitivity analysis, employing various estimation models, largely confirmed the main analysis findings across most parameters. However, inconsistent results were noted for the nasal congestion and eosinophil marker in human studies. Additionally, a sensitivity analysis that excluded studies with a high risk of bias did not affect the outcomes for numerous parameters, though it did impact IL-4 and total IgE in animals as well as total nasal symptoms and eosinophil levels in humans ( Supplementary Table 1 ).

Considerable heterogeneity was observed in approximately half of the analyzed parameters (I 2 =75 − 100%). Exceptions included animal study outcomes for sneezing, and human study parameters such as itching, sneezing, runny nose, total nasal symptom, and quality of life, all of which showed substantial heterogeneity (I 2 =50 − 90%). Conversely, low heterogeneity (I 2 <40%) was found for OVA-specific IgE in animal studies, and for quality of life, total IgE, and eosinophil counts in human studies. To investigate these variations, subgroup analyses based on administration type were performed. While heterogeneity largely persisted for most parameters, notable reductions were observed. Specifically, heterogeneity was reduced for total IgE in animal studies and quality of life in human studies within the oral administration subgroup. In contrast, the topical administration subgroup showed reduced heterogeneity for itching, runny nose, and sneezing in human studies ( Figure 3 , Supplementary Table 2 ).

The quality of evidence for human study parameters varied. For comparisons against a placebo, the certainty of evidence for nasal congestion was assessed as very low. In contrast, evidence for itching, runny nose, sneezing, total nasal symptom, and quality of life was rated as moderate. The certainty for these outcomes was reduced primarily due to inconsistency and imprecision. The evidence for total IgE was considered low quality, with its certainty reduced by imprecision. Notably, the eosinophil marker was supported by high-quality evidence. In comparison with drug groups, the quality of evidence for itching, nasal congestion, runny nose, sneezing, and total nasal symptoms was downgraded due to inconsistency, imprecision, and publication bias ( Supplementary Table 3 ).

This systematic review and meta-analysis, the first to comprehensively evaluate ginger-based formulations for allergic rhinitis, demonstrates multifaceted effects on both symptoms and key immunological markers across animal and human studies. In animal models, ginger-based formulations significantly reduced early-phase symptoms, such as nasal rubbing. It also decreased inflammatory markers including IL-4, IL-5, and OVA-specific IgE, suggesting modulation of the T H 2-driven response and IgE-mediated mast cell activation. In human trials, ginger-based formulations led to significant improvements in itching, runny nose, and sneezing on early-phase symptoms, as well as total nasal symptom scores, and quality of life, accompanied by reductions in eosinophil counts, indicating effects on the late-phase inflammatory response. Patients receiving ginger-based formulations reported greater improvements compared with placebo; however, no significant differences were observed when compared with conventional drugs across symptoms and biomarkers. Collectively, these findings underscore ginger’s therapeutic potential in managing allergic rhinitis, supported by converging evidence from both animal and human studies. Beyond symptomatic improvements observed in animal models, such as reduced nasal rubbing and sneezing (Khaki Vaighan et al. 2024 ), ginger-based formulations significantly modulate allergic responses at cellular and signaling levels (Makchuchit et al. 2017 ; Lalruatfela et al. 2023 ). In cell culture systems, ginger’s bioactive compounds, particularly 6-shogaol, have been shown to inhibit mast cell degranulation by suppressing IgE-sensitized β-hexosaminidase release in RBL-2H3 cells, thereby preventing the rapid release of inflammatory mediators such as histamine (Makchuchit et al. 2017 ; Lalruatfela et al. 2023 ; Khaki Vaighan et al. 2024 ). Furthermore, 6-gingerol suppresses T H 2-associated cytokines, including IL-5, in allergen-sensitized spleen cells, mitigating eosinophilic responses (Lalruatfela et al. 2023 ; Khaki Vaighan et al. 2024 ). While direct effects on IgE levels are more evident in in vivo models, cellular studies suggest that ginger compounds indirectly reduce IgE production by downregulating T H 2 cytokines (e.g., IL-4, IL-13) essential for IgE class switching and B cell activation (Lalruatfela et al. 2023 ; Khaki Vaighan et al. 2024 ). Additionally, 6-gingerol influences T cell receptor-mediated signal transduction by inhibiting mitogen-activated protein kinases (MAPKs), calcium release, and nuclear localization of fos proto-oncogene (c-fos) and nuclear factor kappa B (NF-κB), pathways crucial for T cell activation and proliferation (Lalruatfela et al. 2023 ; Khaki Vaighan et al. 2024 ). Collectively, these cellular and molecular interactions illustrate how ginger attenuates inflammatory mediators such as IL-5 and contributes to the reduction of IgE-mediated allergic responses. In animal studies, oral ginger-based formulations have been shown to effectively reduce IL-4, IL-5, and allergen-specific IgE levels. During the sensitization phase of the allergic response, effector cells release cytokines, including IL-4, which plays a pivotal role in driving the differentiation of naive T cells into T H 2 cells and stimulating B cells to produce allergen-specific IgE (Ahui et al. 2008 ). While IL-5 may begin to be released during this phase, its vital role lies in promoting the subsequent infiltration of inflammatory cells, notably eosinophils, basophils, and T cells, from the systemic circulation into the nasal submucosa. This process underlies the transition to the late-phase inflammatory response (Ohnishi et al. 1993 ; Drazdauskaitė et al. 2020 ). By suppressing mast cell activation, ginger-based formulations can alleviate early-phase symptoms such as nasal rubbing, even though they may not significantly alter total IgE levels. This targeted modulation of specific inflammatory pathways highlights the therapeutic potential of ginger-based formulations in managing allergic rhinitis. In human studies, ginger-based formulations have demonstrated multifaceted effects on allergic rhinitis. They significantly reduced a range of symptoms, including itching, runny nose, and sneezing, leading to overall improvements in total nasal symptom scores compared with placebo (Laursen et al. 2023 , 2020 ). Beyond symptom alleviation, ginger-based formulations also modulated key inflammatory pathways. Notably, they significantly reduced eosinophil counts, critical effector cells in the late-phase allergic response, even when compared with placebo (Pawankar et al. 2011 ). However, no significant changes in total IgE levels were observed, suggesting that ginger primarily acts on downstream inflammatory processes (e.g., eosinophil recruitment and activity), rather than broadly suppressing systemic IgE production that initiates the allergic cascade. Moreover, participants receiving ginger-based formulations reported significant improvements in quality of life compared with placebo, consistent with the observed reductions in symptoms and modulation of inflammatory markers. Effective symptom control and decreased inflammation are well-established contributors to enhanced quality of life in allergic rhinitis (Moitra et al. 2023 ). Regarding the route of administration in humans, oral ginger-based formulations demonstrated more consistent benefits for allergic rhinitis than topical preparations, likely due to superior systemic bioavailability of bioactive compounds such as 6-gingerol and 6-shogaol (Stielow et al. 2023 ). It is also important to consider that proven effective topical treatments for allergic rhinitis namely intranasal corticosteroid sprays achieve high local drug concentrations right at the nasal mucosa, while minimizing systemic exposure (Salib and Howarth 2003 ). Topical application in some studies that involves placing ginger on acupuncture points through the skin does not directly target the nasal passages and likely results in subtherapeutic concentrations at the site of inflammation. This discrepancy in drug delivery routes may explain why oral ginger demonstrates more consistent benefits in allergic rhinitis than such non-direct topical approaches. Taken together, these findings indicate that ginger, particularly in oral formulations, may serve as an effective adjunctive therapy for allergic rhinitis, with both symptomatic and immunological improvements mediated through anti-inflammatory and immunomodulatory mechanisms. However, the meta-analysis comparing ginger-based formulations with conventional drugs for allergic rhinitis found no significant difference in the reduction of all allergic symptoms. While this may suggest that ginger-based formulations could exert effects comparable to conventional drugs, the available evidence does not allow a conclusion of non-inferiority or equivalence. One study specifically investigated the efficacy of ginger extract against loratadine (Yamprasert et al. 2020 ). The results showed no statistically significant difference in the change of total nasal symptom scores between the ginger and loratadine groups, indicating that ginger extract may have potential as an alternative herbal therapy for alleviating allergic rhinitis symptoms, but further well-designed trials are needed to establish comparative efficacy. Regarding safety, previous studies of ginger-based formulations for allergic rhinitis reported no significant changes in liver function markers (ALP, ALT, AST) or kidney function (BUN) compared with drug groups (Houngiam and Waipoj Chanvimalueng 2018 ; Yamprasert et al. 2020 ; Lee et al. 2024 ). These findings suggest that ginger interventions are generally well-tolerated and do not adversely affect these vital organ functions, supporting a favorable safety profile for their use (National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases 2012 ). This study has several limitations. First, most of the evaluated ginger-based formulations were multi-ingredient rather than isolated ginger, making it difficult to attribute the observed efficacy specifically to ginger, as potential synergistic effects from other components cannot be excluded. Accordingly, the proposed mechanistic interpretations, although supported by the known bioactivity of ginger, should be interpreted with caution, as other components within the formulations may also contribute to the observed effects on allergic rhinitis-related pathways. Second, many studies did not adequately report details on intervention dose, preparation, or formulation type, which limits reproducibility and precludes dose-response or formulation-based subgroup analyses. Third, only limited number of studies investigated cytokine and signaling outcomes in both animal and human studies, leaving the precise mechanisms of ginger-based formulations on these pathways insufficiently characterized. Fourth, heterogeneity was high for most outcomes and persisted despite subgroup analyses. This heterogeneity may be explained by differences in formulation composition (including multiple components and the proportion of ginger), as well as inconsistencies in dosing regimens and intervention duration across studies. Nevertheless, the moderate quality of evidence for key allergic rhinitis outcomes, as determined by the GRADE approach, suggests that these findings should be interpreted with caution, while still providing preliminary evidence to inform clinical decision-making regarding ginger-based formulations. Overall, this study offers a useful foundation for researchers considering such formulations as a potential therapeutic option. Future studies should further investigate ginger, across its various formulations, with particular emphasis on oral administration. Given the variability in composition and preparation methods observed in current studies, future research should prioritize the use of well-characterized ginger extracts with defined bioactive constituents to improve consistency and comparability. In addition, more mechanistic studies are needed to elucidate the underlying biological pathways, particularly those involving key cytokine signaling networks associated with allergic rhinitis.

Ginger-based formulations show promise as a therapeutic option for allergic rhinitis, with evidence from both animal and human studies demonstrating improvements in clinical symptoms and modulation of key immunological markers. However, ginger alone may not fully account for these effects, as many interventions are multi-component; the observed benefits likely reflect the combined effects of overall formulations. Future studies should focus on prioritize standardized ginger extracts, with a focus on elucidating underlying mechanisms, particularly key cytokine signaling pathways, and clarifying the specific contribution of ginger to the alleviation of allergic rhinitis symptoms.
